opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think my view has changed quite a lot over the years. When I was a PhD student, a Best Paper award felt like this ultimate stamp of validation, something that would tell you, "Yes, you've made it, your work matters." And of course it's a wonderful honor, and I'm grateful whenever the community recognizes something we've done.

But now I see it much more as a byproduct than a goal. If you look back at the history of awards at CVPR or ICCV or NeurIPS, many of the papers that really shaped the field didn't win anything at the time, and some award-winning papers are now largely forgotten. Awards reflect the taste of a particular committee in a particular year. That's useful information, but it's noisy, and it's very short-term.

What I care about more is whether the work survives time. Five years later, do people still build on it? Does it change how people think about a problem, or does it just push a number on a benchmark? Something like ResNet or the Transformer: their impact came from the ideas being simple, general, and correct, not from a trophy.

I also tell my students: if you optimize for awards, you'll tend to optimize for what looks impressive to reviewers right now. You chase the hot topic, make the story flashy, oversell a bit. That can actually pull you away from the deeper, riskier questions that could matter much more. I'd rather they work on something they truly believe is important, even if it's unfashionable, and do it really carefully and honestly.

So if an award comes, great, celebrate it, have dinner with the team. But it shouldn't be the compass. The compass should be your own curiosity and your judgment about what problems are actually worth solving.

r001.rationale: The response says awards reflect a committee’s taste in a particular year and are noisy, while noting that influential papers may not win. This communicates that an award does not necessarily reflect research quality.

r002.rationale: The response calls awards “noisy” and short-term, but does not characterize the selection process as highly random.

r003.rationale: The response says an award should be a byproduct rather than a goal or compass, and warns that optimizing for awards can pull researchers away from important questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my view has changed a lot. When I was a PhD student, a Best Paper felt like the ultimate validation, the thing you quietly dreamed about. And I've been lucky to be on papers that got that kind of recognition, so I know how good it feels in the moment.

But the longer I've done this, the more I think awards are a noisy signal. A committee of a few people is looking at a snapshot, often before anyone really knows what the work will mean. Some of the most influential papers in our field were rejected at first or got no award at all. ResNet is a good example of a paper that was recognized early, but plenty of ideas that changed everything, like the transformer or even early work on diffusion, didn't get that kind of spotlight when they came out. The real judgment comes from the community over years: does anyone build on it, does it change how people think, do students still read it five years later.

So now I try not to optimize for awards at all. If you aim for a Best Paper, you tend to write papers that look like Best Papers, with a clean story and a safe, impressive result. That often pushes you away from the messy, uncertain problems where the real progress happens. I'd much rather pursue a question I find genuinely confusing, where I'm not sure what the answer will be. If that work turns out to matter, recognition may come, or it may not, and either way it's fine.

The thing I tell my students is: treat the award as a side effect, never the goal. The goal is to understand something you didn't before and to leave the field a little clearer than you found it. If you keep doing that honestly, you'll build taste, and taste is worth far more than any trophy.

r001.rationale: It calls awards a “noisy signal” and notes that influential work may receive no award, making clear that an award does not reliably reflect research quality.

r002.rationale: It describes awards as a noisy signal and mentions small committees and early judgments, but does not clearly characterize the selection process as highly random.

r003.rationale: It says researchers should not optimize for awards and tells students to treat an award as a side effect, never the goal.

astra-6.text:
I think of Best Paper awards as a nice bonus, but not a very good objective. You can control whether you’re working on a meaningful problem, whether you’re being rigorous, and whether you’re willing to follow an idea that might not work. You can’t really control how a committee responds to it.

And the timescales are different. An award is a judgment at the moment a paper comes out. The impact of that work might only become clear several years later. Sometimes those judgments line up, and sometimes they don’t.

Of course, recognition feels good. I don’t want to pretend it doesn’t matter. But if you start asking, “What would win Best Paper?” it can distort your taste. I’d rather ask, “Is this something we need to understand? And would I still be excited to work on it if it didn’t get an award?”

r001.rationale: The response says committee reactions are uncontrollable and may differ from later judgments of impact, but it does not state that an award may fail to reflect research quality.

r002.rationale: Calling committee response uncontrollable does not characterize award selection as highly random.

r003.rationale: The response calls awards a poor objective, says focusing on what would win can distort research taste, and favors pursuing meaningful questions instead.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s dangerous to make Best Paper an objective. It’s a nice recognition, and of course you’re happy when your work gets recognized. But an award reflects what a particular committee values at a particular moment. That’s different from whether the work will matter five or ten years later.

As a researcher, you want to develop your own judgment: Is this an important question? Am I learning something? Could this change how people approach a problem? Those are much better things to pursue. If an award comes, that’s wonderful. But it should be a byproduct, not the thing that determines what you work on.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes committee recognition at a particular moment from whether the work will matter later, conveying that an award does not necessarily reflect research quality.

r002.rationale: It says award choices reflect a committee’s values at a particular moment, but does not characterize selection as highly random.

r003.rationale: It explicitly calls making Best Paper an objective dangerous and says awards should be a byproduct, not what determines the work.
